stem: A student answers: 'Predictive AI is judged on accuracy; generative AI is judged on creativity.' Which correction turns this into a full-mark answer?
choices: Swap them: generative AI is the one judged on accuracy, because it must reproduce its training data
Replace 'creativity' with 'novelty': generative AI is judged on how different its output is from the training data
Replace 'creativity' with 'plausible context relevance', and make 'accuracy' specifically accuracy against verifiable ground truths
Nothing needs changing; accuracy versus creativity is the course's own distinction
explanation: The course's wording is the mark: predictive AI is evaluated on accuracy against verifiable ground truths (an MLP classifier), generative AI on plausible context relevance (GPT). 'Creativity' and 'novelty' are the tempting paraphrases, and neither is the standard the course names.

stem: Select all the statements that describe predictive AI rather than generative AI.
choices: It learns a mapping x → y, then you crank the input
It learns a mapping z → x, then you crank the pseudo-random number generator
It asks 'What WILL be?'
It models the data distribution p(x), or p(x|c) when conditioned
It is judged on accuracy against verifiable ground truths
explanation: Predictive: learn x → y and crank the input, ask what WILL be, score against ground truth. The z → x map cranked by the PRNG and the model of p(x) are the generative side — 'what COULD be?'.

stem: The question says 'give one example of each'. Which pairing of examples is correct?
choices: Predictive: GPT; generative: an MLP classifier
Predictive: an MLP classifier, or cluster analysis; generative: GPT
Predictive: a diffusion model; generative: a CNN image classifier
Predictive: cluster analysis; generative: a CNN, because it produces feature maps
explanation: The 2024 model answer gives an MLP (supervised) and cluster analysis (unsupervised) as predictive examples and GPT as the generative one. A CNN classifier is predictive even though it computes feature maps: producing intermediate numbers is not generating new content.

stem: Which grouping of the course's six foundational architectures into its three stages is right?
choices: Predict: MLP, CNN · Represent: VAE, U-Net · Generate: Transformer, Diffusion
Predict: MLP, CNN, U-Net · Represent: VAE · Generate: Transformer, GAN
Predict: MLP · Represent: CNN, VAE · Generate: U-Net, Transformer, Diffusion
Predict: MLP, CNN · Represent: Transformer, U-Net · Generate: VAE, Diffusion
explanation: MLP and CNN predict ('what is most likely?'), VAE and U-Net form the representation bridge ('what is the underlying structure?'), Transformer and Diffusion generate ('what could be?'). The GAN is part of the story but is not one of the six.

stem: Fill the gap in the course's list of six architectures, in order: MLP, CNN, VAE, ____, Transformer, Diffusion.
explanation: U-Net, the encoder-decoder CNN whose skip connections carry fine spatial detail across the bottleneck — the other half of the representation bridge with the VAE. It is the one of the six students most often forget.

stem: Asked to tell the U-Net apart from a plain encoder-decoder, which clause earns the mark?
choices: It compresses the input to a narrower bottleneck than any other encoder-decoder
It encodes each input to a probability distribution rather than a point
It replaces convolution with attention in the decoder half
Skip connections carry fine spatial detail from each encoder stage across to the matching decoder stage
explanation: The skip connections are what make the U: detail destroyed on the way down is handed straight across, which is why U-Nets suit segmentation and medical imaging. Encoding to a distribution is the VAE's distinguishing clause, not the U-Net's.

stem: Which sentence states the relationship between gradient descent and backpropagation the way the course wants it?
choices: Backpropagation computes the gradient and gradient descent then checks whether the prediction was right
Backpropagation is a specialisation of the gradient descent algorithm, applied to minimise prediction error for a multilayer perceptron by tweaking its weights and biases
Backpropagation is an alternative to gradient descent that finds the minimum in one analytic step
Gradient descent is a specialisation of backpropagation for networks with a single layer
explanation: This is the 'exam sentence' dictated in class; learn it verbatim. The direction of specialisation is the trap: backprop is the special case (an MLP, error sent backwards through the layers), gradient descent is the general optimiser.

stem: A student writes: 'Gradient descent follows the gradient downhill to the minimum.' What is wrong with it?
choices: Nothing; that is the definition
Gradient descent does not use the gradient at all; it tries random steps
It should say 'to the global minimum', which gradient descent is guaranteed to reach
The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent, so the algorithm steps against it, a small step at a time, repeatedly
explanation: The gradient points uphill; training takes small steps against it and recomputes, iteratively. The distinguishing clause is 'against the gradient', and the method only ever settles in a local minimum, so 'guaranteed global minimum' is also wrong.

stem: Backpropagation is one of the gradient-descent variants, alongside stochastic gradient descent, momentum and Adam.
choices: True
False
explanation: False. SGD, mini-batch, momentum, RMSProp and Adam are variants of the optimiser. Backpropagation is how the gradient they all consume is computed, so it sits underneath every one of them.

stem: In one clause, what separates a variational autoencoder from a plain autoencoder?
choices: The VAE encodes each input to a probability distribution over the latent space rather than to one fixed point
The VAE has no bottleneck, so it keeps every detail of the input
The VAE is trained with labelled data, the autoencoder without
The VAE adds skip connections between the encoder and the decoder
explanation: Point versus distribution. Because the VAE's encoder outputs a distribution, the latent space is filled in continuously and a randomly drawn point still decodes to something realistic. Skip connections are the U-Net; neither kind of autoencoder needs labels.

stem: A plain autoencoder's decoder will turn any latent code into an output. Why is it still not a generator?
choices: Its decoder is deleted after training, so nothing can produce new outputs
It can only produce outputs the same size as its inputs
Nothing trained the space between the codes of real examples, so a randomly chosen point may decode to nonsense; the VAE forces the codes into a distribution you can sample from
It produces exact copies of training images, which is prediction by definition
explanation: Generation is sampling. A plain AE only learned codes for the inputs it was given, so its latent space has holes. The VAE's regularisation fills them, so 'sample z, then decode' yields a new, realistic example never in the training set.

stem: The examiner's lab slide asked 'What is a ____ space?' One word: the compressed internal representation at an autoencoder's bottleneck.
explanation: Latent. The latent space is the learned, compressed representation in which each point stands for an input and nearby points stand for similar inputs. Its continuity is what makes moving through it, and sampling from it in a VAE, meaningful.

stem: 'How does the transformer decide which word it generates next?' Which answer earns the mark?
choices: It looks up which word most often followed the previous word in its training text and copies it
It compresses the prompt into one fixed vector and decodes the most likely sentence from it
Attention finds the single most similar word in the prompt and repeats it

It embeds and positionally encodes the tokens, uses attention to weigh how much each token should inform the others, and outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary from which the next token is sampled
explanation: Embed, position, attend, then a distribution over the whole vocabulary and a sample from it. The first choice is a Markov chain, the second is the fixed bottleneck attention replaced. Sampling is why the same prompt can give different answers.

stem: In 'she sat on the bank of the river', which mechanism pulls 'bank' towards the shore rather than the vault, and why not the other one?
choices: Attention, because it gives each word a local-context interpretation from the other words in this sentence; the embedding of 'bank' is the same wherever the word appears
The embedding, because it stores a separate vector for every sense of every word
Positional encoding, because 'river' comes after 'bank'
The softmax, because it chooses the most probable meaning
explanation: Embedding = global-context meaning (the vocabulary); attention = local-context interpretation (the grammar). One embedding per token is the point: it cannot know which sentence it is in. Positional encoding supplies order, not meaning.

stem: Where does the T in GPT come from?
choices: Vaswani and colleagues' 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', which dropped recurrence and convolution and kept attention
Turing's 1950 paper, which proposed the imitation game
Mikolov's 2013 word2vec, which turned words into vectors
Goodfellow's 2014 paper, which made 'generative' famous
explanation: The Transformer, Vaswani et al. 2017. It sits on the language timeline after word2vec (2013) and before GPT (2018). Word2vec supplied embeddings; the Transformer supplied attention without recurrence, which is what made internet-scale pre-training possible.

stem: In Hubel and Wiesel's experiment, what did the cat's striate-cortex neurons respond to?
choices: The picture of a mouse projected on the slide
Any change in overall brightness, whatever its shape
Oriented lines, such as the straight edge of the slide, rather than whole objects
Faces, which were later found to have their own dedicated region
explanation: The famous accident: the neurons fired at the edge of the slide being pushed in, not at the picture on it. Line detectors combine into curves, shapes and objects — the hierarchy of features the Neocognitron and the CNN copy. Say 'around 1959' for the date.

stem: Early layers of a trained CNN respond to edges; deep layers respond to whole objects. Which pair names the mechanism and the biological finding it mirrors?
choices: Dropout, mirroring the brain's forgetting of unused connections
The receptive field widening with depth, mirroring the cat's line detectors combining upward into shapes and objects
Softmax, mirroring the brain's choice between competing objects
Positional encoding, mirroring the retina's map of where things are
explanation: Each layer pools from the one below, so a deeper neuron sees a larger region of the image and can represent an object rather than an edge. That is Hubel and Wiesel's hierarchy of features — lines to curves to shapes to objects — built into the architecture.

stem: A digit recogniser built as a plain MLP breaks when the digit moves to another part of the image. What single change fixes it, and why?
choices: Add more hidden layers, so the network has enough capacity to memorise every position
Switch the activation from sigmoid to ReLU, so gradients flow further
Add dropout, so the network cannot rely on any one pixel
Slide the same learned filters over every region, so a feature is detected wherever it sits — weight sharing, which gives translational covariance
explanation: An MLP gives every pixel position its own weight, so a shifted digit is a completely different input. A convolutional layer shares one filter across all positions, so the response simply shifts with the feature. More depth, ReLU and dropout do not touch the position problem.

stem: Applying the same learned filter at every position in the image is called weight ____.
explanation: Weight sharing. It is why a CNN detects a feature wherever it appears (translational covariance) and why its parameter count does not grow with image size.

stem: 'Why did mobile phones start recognising images in the 2010s?' Select all three things the answer must name.
choices: Large labelled datasets such as ImageNet
The Transformer, which let phones attend to every pixel at once
GPU compute fast enough for the matrix multiplications
Deep convolutional architectures, as AlexNet showed in 2012
Better hand-written rules describing what a cat or a face looks like
explanation: Data, compute and architecture converged; naming only one loses the mark. The Transformer came in 2017 and was not the vision story of the early 2010s, and hand-written rules are exactly what failed — a face that moves or changes lighting breaks them.

stem: Which sentence gets ImageNet and AlexNet the right way round?
choices: ImageNet is the large labelled image collection built by Fei-Fei Li; AlexNet is the 2012 CNN that cut its error rate from about 25% to single digits
AlexNet is the labelled dataset; ImageNet is the 2012 network trained on it
ImageNet and AlexNet are two names for the same 2012 competition
ImageNet is Fukushima's 1980 network; AlexNet is its 2012 successor
explanation: Dataset versus model is the classic confusion. ImageNet (Fei-Fei Li, 2010 onward) is the data and the competition; AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton) is the network entered into it. Fukushima's 1980 network is the Neocognitron.

stem: What does a single artificial neuron (perceptron) compute?
choices: It multiplies all its inputs together and outputs the largest
It takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes it through an activation, firing once the threshold is passed
It stores the most recent input and repeats it to the next layer
It compares its input with every stored training example and outputs the closest
explanation: Weighted sum plus bias, then activation: the perceptron is a mathematical model of a neuron that fires past an internal threshold. The weights scale each input; the bias shifts the threshold.

stem: A perceptron has two inputs and one output. How many trainable parameters does it have, and what are they?
choices: Two: one weight per input
Four: two inputs, one output and one bias
Three: two weights and one bias
One: the threshold
explanation: Two inputs, one output, three parameters — the example dictated in class. One weight per incoming connection plus one bias per neuron. Inputs are data you supply, so they never count; forgetting the bias gives the tempting 'two'.

stem: A single perceptron can learn AND and OR but not XOR. Which clause explains why a hidden layer is needed?
choices: XOR needs more training examples than one perceptron can store
XOR outputs negative numbers, which a perceptron cannot produce
XOR requires recurrence, which only an RNN has
XOR is not linearly separable, and one perceptron can only draw one straight boundary
explanation: One perceptron draws one line; AND and OR can be separated by a line, XOR cannot. Stacking layers bends the boundary, which is the whole argument for the multilayer perceptron — the limitation Minsky and Papert made famous in 1969.

stem: Turing's imitation game, Business Intelligence and Computational Intelligence each illustrate a different sense of 'intelligence'. Which set of senses matches them, in that order?
choices: Human-like · advantageous information · solution path to a problem
Artifact · artificial semblance · artful creation
Solution path · human-like · advantageous information
Recognition · prediction · generation
explanation: Human-like (Turing), advantageous information of tactical value (military or business intelligence), and a solution path or optimal method (computational or digital intelligence). Artifact, semblance and artful creation are the three senses of the A, not the I.

stem: Select all three senses the course gives to the A in 'AI'.
choices: Autonomous — acting without human input
Artful creation — 'truth manufactured'
Advantageous information — as in business intelligence
Artifact or artifice — a machine creation made by humans
Artificial semblance — when 'seems about right' will do
explanation: Artifact/artifice, artificial semblance and artful creation. Advantageous information is a sense of the I, the classic cross-over trap; autonomy is a property AI systems may have, not what the letter stands for.

stem: 'In what way is ML larger than AI, and in what way is AI larger than ML?' Which answer earns both halves?
choices: ML is simply a subset of AI, so AI is larger in every way
ML reaches outside AI through data-driven calibration in statistics, optimisation and forecasting; AI reaches outside ML through rule-based GOFAI, search and planning that involve no learning
AI is a subset of ML, because every AI system today is trained on data
They are the same field under two names
explanation: Neither contains the other; they overlap. The trap is the textbook 'ML ⊂ AI' diagram, which answers only half the question. Each half needs its own example.

stem: Which example shows AI being larger than machine learning?
choices: A linear regression that forecasts next month's sales
A CNN trained to classify X-rays
An expert system of hand-written if-then rules for diagnosing infections
A clustering algorithm that segments customers
explanation: The expert system is AI with no learning from data at all, so it sits outside ML. The regression and the clustering are ML used well outside anything called AI (the other direction), and the CNN is in both.

stem: 'What is symbolic AI (not neural networks)? Expert systems?' Which answer fits two lines and earns the mark?
choices: Early neural networks such as the perceptron, which used symbols as inputs
AI that learns rules automatically from labelled data, as decision trees do
Hand-written if-then rules over symbols with no learning from data, e.g. MYCIN (1975) diagnosing bacterial infections at about 65% accuracy; later retronymed GOFAI
Language models that reason with logical symbols, such as GPT
explanation: Rule-based formal logic, written by hand, no learning: that is the distinguishing clause. MYCIN is the example to name, with LISP and Prolog as its languages. It stalled into the AI winter and was renamed GOFAI once neural AI took the name.

stem: Symbolic, rule-based AI was given a retronym once neural approaches took the name 'AI'. What is it? (acronym or expansion)
explanation: GOFAI, Good Old-Fashioned AI. A retronym is a new name for an old thing, forced because something newer took the original name — the same move later turned ordinary AI into 'predictive AI'.

stem: Training error keeps falling while validation error starts to rise. What is happening, and which remedy from the assigned CNN course addresses it?
choices: Underfitting; add dropout so more units are active
Overfitting; remove the validation set so training can continue
Underfitting; make the network larger
Overfitting; add dropout, which randomly switches off units during training so no single path is relied on
explanation: The gap opening between the curves is overfitting; both errors staying high would be underfitting. Dropout is a regulariser: because any unit may vanish on any pass, the network must spread its representation instead of memorising through one route. Data augmentation is the other named fix.

stem: Which pairing of CNN layer to job is wrong?
choices: ReLU — introduces nonlinearity, returning the input if positive and zero otherwise
Pooling — reduces the size of the representation
Softmax — turns raw activations into a probability distribution over the classes
Cross-entropy — randomly switches off units during training to prevent overfitting
explanation: Cross-entropy is the loss: the distance between the predicted class probabilities and the true one-hot label. Randomly switching off units is dropout. The other three pairings are the course's own definitions.

stem: The examiner's bonus question: 'Can we have generative AI without neural networks?' Which answer earns the mark?
choices: No: generation is defined as something only neural networks can do
Yes in principle: a Markov chain generates text from next-token statistics; but without a learned representation it has no context, so output is locally plausible and globally incoherent
Yes, and the results match GPT, because generation only needs a large enough table of word counts
No: before neural networks, computers could only follow if-then rules
explanation: Yes on the definition, no in practice. Any sampler from a fitted distribution is generative; what the neural network adds is context. The mark sits in the second clause — why the non-neural version falls short.

stem: In a diffusion model, which process is learned and what does generation start from?
choices: Both the noising and the denoising are learned; generation starts from a training image
The noising is learned and the denoising is fixed; generation starts from a text prompt alone
The forward noising is fixed by design and only the reverse denoising is learned; generation starts from pure noise and denoises step by step
Neither is learned; the model looks up the closest training image to the noise
explanation: Prescribed forward, learned reverse. Because the noise was added deliberately, the true noise at every step is known, which supervises the denoiser. Generation begins from pure noise, optionally guided by a text embedding. A VAE, by contrast, learns both directions.

stem: What is ironic about the GAN's place in the history of generative AI?
choices: It was designed to generate images, but turned out to be better at classifying them
It was the first neural network, but was forgotten for fifty years
It was invented for text, but only ever worked on images
The adversarial setup was built to sharpen a predictive discriminator, and the generator ended up being the star
explanation: The generator was supposed to feed the discriminator harder cases. Deepfakes made the generator famous instead, and 'generative' took its modern meaning from this architecture (Goodfellow, 2014) before GPT inherited the word.

stem: Why is AI slop an economic problem and not only a quality problem?
choices: Because the old web paid creators through clicks and ads, and AI search now answers without a visit, so the incentive to produce trustworthy content evaporates
Because generating it costs more electricity than human writing
Because AI companies charge creators to have their content indexed
Because advertisers refuse to place ads beside any AI-generated text
explanation: The broken payment loop: no visit, no ad revenue, no one funding quality material — which also degrades the content supply the models were trained on. Countermeasures are limited, so the consumer has to stay vigilant.
